chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a group of people who fasted the month of Ramadan, and a black cloud covered them at the time of sunset, so they thought it was night and broke their fast. Then the cloud cleared, and behold, the sun was still there.
He (peace be upon him) said: Upon the one who broke the fast is the making up (qada') of that day's fast.
Indeed, Allah (Mighty and Majestic) says: 'Complete the fasting until the night.'
So whoever eats before the night enters, upon him is its making up, because he ate deliberately.

key_terms.إِلَى اللَّيْلِ: Until the night (the Quranic endpoint for the daily fast)
key_terms.صِيَامُ: Fasting (the act of abstaining from food/drink during daylight hours)
key_terms.قَضَاؤُهُ: Its making up (qada', the obligation to make up a missed fast later)
key_terms.مُتَعَمِّداً: Deliberately/intentionally (indicating the act was not due to ignorance of the law but error in fact)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for someone who breaks their fast because they mistakenly thought it was night due to a cloud?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the distinction between *qada'* (make-up) and *kaffarah* (expiation) in cases of mistaken fasting, ruling that breaking the fast due to a genuine error like a black cloud incurs only *qada'*, not the heavier penalty for deliberate pre-dawn eating. It underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the entry of night is determined by actual astronomical reality rather than subjective perception, aligning with the literal interpretation of 'until night' in the Quran. This ruling highlights the balance between strict adherence to divine commands and the leniency granted for reasonable human error in ritual practice.
